ask.text: How should the app that uses the table tell it which look to use? ZestTabs just follows a 'dark' class that the app puts on the page (body.dark) and has no setting of its own. For the table, do you want that same approach, a setting you pass to the table (for example theme="dark" | "light" | "system"), or both?
ask.why: It decides whether the table gets a new public setting (and how apps with several tables can differ) or only reacts to something the app already does, and it decides how 'system' (follow the device's light/dark choice) is expressed.

options.label: Both: a theme setting on the table, and when it is not given the table follows body.dark like ZestTabs
options.consequence: Apps can force one table dark/light/system, and apps that already toggle body.dark work with no code change. Existing users see no change unless they opt in.

options.label: Only a theme setting on the table (light, dark, system)
options.consequence: Clear and explicit, but apps that already toggle body.dark must pass the setting to every table.

options.label: Only follow body.dark like ZestTabs (no setting)
options.consequence: Matches ZestTabs exactly, but there is no 'system' mode unless the app itself sets body.dark from the device preference.

coverage.note: Control mechanism for the owner app not yet decided.
No data stored by the library; theme choice is a prop/page state owned by the app.
Presentation-only change; no records or ownership.
Unknown theme value falls back to the default; to be written up after the mechanism is chosen.
Loading skeleton, empty, no-more-data, spinner and detail rows must follow the active theme.
Styling only; no change to row counts, sorting or paging.
No personal data; the library must not store the theme choice itself.
Accessible contrast in both themes, no flash of wrong theme in Next.js, no bundle growth beyond CSS.
